Paragraph: In Bhagavad Gita Chapter 18, Verse 37, Krishna explains authentic happiness: 'That which seems like poison in the beginning but tastes like nectar in the end—born of the serene self-realization of one's intellect—that happiness is said to be in the mode of goodness (Sattva).'
Situation/Problem_Faced: Avoidance of difficult self-discipline in favor of short-term gratification, leading to long-term suffering.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Krishna clarifies that meaningful growth requires enduring initial discomfort (poison) to reap sustainable well-being (nectar).
Outcome/Resolution: Embracing short-term discomfort yields long-term mental clarity and fulfillment.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Sattvika Sukha (Pure happiness derived from mental clarity and self-discipline)
Shreyas vs. Preyas (Choosing long-term good over short-term pleasure)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Spiritual joy requires self-discipline that may feel challenging initially, but yields eternal peace.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Directly correlates with delayed gratification, impulse control, and long-term goal orientation.
